content: 1. There were no significant inconsistencies, imprecisions, or publication biases identified in the studies. However, there was serious indirectness in some cases. The age of participants ranged from 18 to 66 years, with women comprising less than 30% of the sample. Physical activity (PA) interventions were conducted at least three times per week for durations ranging from 6 to 16 weeks. 2. Nine out of ten studies assessed weight and/or body composition. Six meta-analyses were performed to evaluate body composition. Participants in the progressive resistance exercise (PRE) or combined PRE and aerobic exercise intervention groups showed improvements in body composition compared to the non-exercising control group. Many participants in the individual studies were diagnosed with AIDS-related wasting syndrome, and increases in body composition were interpreted as favorable outcomes. 3. Heterogeneity in the results may have been due to differences in the methods used to measure arm and thigh girth across studies. The other five meta-analyses on body composition showed no significant differences between groups. 4. Seven out of thirteen studies assessed lean body mass, with resistance training (RT) interventions lasting 12 to 24 weeks, performed at least three times per week. The effect size for lean body mass after progressive resistance training was quantified using Hedges’ g. However, the quality of the included studies for lean body mass was low, with a PEDro score of 5, leaving room for potential biases and limiting the generalizability of the results. 5. Moderate evidence was found for the effects of multimodal exercise interventions. Five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 253 participants were included, with intervention durations ranging from 12 to 24 weeks, performed at least three times per week for a minimum of 20 minutes. All five studies assessed body fat percentage, showing reductions in body fat percentage, trunk fat, and limb fat, along with increases in lean mass in response to aerobic and concurrent training. 6. One high-quality study demonstrated a significant decrease in body fat percentage following aerobic training. However, limitations included the lack of heterogeneity testing and small sample sizes. As a result, it is difficult to conclusively determine the effects of physical training on body composition, necessitating further studies with validated methods to investigate the impact of different training types on body composition in individuals with HIV-associated lipodystrophy. 7. The quality of evidence for body composition outcomes was downgraded to moderate or low in several cases due to attrition bias, performance bias, and lack of blinding. For example, lean body mass, leg muscle area, and waist circumference were downgraded to low due to high risks of performance bias across studies. Arm and thigh girth outcomes were initially rated very low but were upgraded to moderate due to evidence of a dose-response relationship. 8. Physical activity interventions were associated with improvements in anxiety and depression among people living with HIV. Aerobic exercise interventions, lasting 5 to 52 weeks and performed three times per week for 20 to 120 minutes, showed clinically significant improvements in depression-dejection scores compared to non-exercising controls. However, the risk of bias was serious in some studies. 9. Resistance exercise interventions were not systematically reviewed, but multimodal exercise interventions showed significant improvements in depression and anxiety. For example, a meta-analysis of ten RCTs with 479 participants found significant reductions in depression and anxiety scores in favor of the exercise group compared to controls. 10. Physical activity interventions also improved fitness and functional capacity among people living with HIV. Aerobic exercise interventions, lasting 6 to 52 weeks and performed three times per week for 20 to 120 minutes, significantly improved VO2 max in five out of six meta-analyses. These findings highlight the potential benefits of physical activity for improving both mental and physical health outcomes in this population.
